newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-Totta seen cheap in privatisation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Totta seen cheap in privatisation.

text.p: Investors will snap up shares in Banco Totta e Acores when the Portuguese state sells off its 13.22 percent stake in the bank later this year because they are cheap and have good growth prospects, analysts said on Friday.

The Socialist government of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres is expected to sell the stake next month, in the last bank privatisation this year, after it earned $900 million from the sale of Banco de Fomento e Exterior in August.
The selloffs are part of the government's ambitious privatisation programme that could bring in at least $450 million to state coffers this year and a similar sum in 1997.
Totta is a commercial bank belonging to 78-year-old Antonio Champalimaud, Portugal's richest man, who owns Portugal's third biggest banking group.
Champalimaud's insurer Mundial Confianca is the holding company for Totta and another commercial bank, Banco Pinto & Sotto Mayor (BPSM), as well as investment bank Banco Chemical (Portugal).
The cabinet said late on Thursday that it planned to sell 6.3 million shares, 80 percent of the state holding, by national and international direct sale.

It would also sell some 1.6 million shares in Totta via a public offer for sale (OPV) on the Lisbon bourse. These included 635,000 shares for employees, 465,000 for small investors and emigrants, and 500,000 for the general public.
"The privatisation should go well," said Rodrigo Guimaraes, partner with Lisbon broker Midas.
"I would be surprised if Totta is priced at much above what it is trading for now," he added.

Trade in Totta shares was suspended by Lisbon bourse on Friday after Diario Economico paper quoted a source close to Totta's board as saying government advisers had valued the shares to be sold at the coming privatisation at 3,000 escudos.
Totta shares closed at 2,740 escudos on Thursday.
Mark Howard, analyst with Lloyds Bank Fund Managers, said that 3,000 escudos would be a cheap privatisation price, even though it is a premium to the present market price.
"There aren't many opportunities to buy into a bank privatisation, and Totta is certainly a quality bank," he said.
A privatisation price of 3,000 escudos would bring in some $23.7 billion escudos ($154 million).
Analysts said Totta shares were cheap because the market had penalised them this year after a series of unimpressive results as the bank reduced its non-performing loan portfolio.

Totta posted a consolidated net profit of 8.4 billion escudos in the first six months of 1996, down from 11.7 billion in the same year-ago period. The bank said it had increased provisions for bad loans.
Forecasts of three analysts polled by Reuters for Totta's 1996 profits ranged from 16.5 to 18.1 billion escudos and for 1997 from 16.9 to 18.8 billion escudos.

Analysts said the bank had good growth prospects based on cost cutting, its active involvement in the home loans business during a climate of falling interest rates, and its commitment to corporate lending as the economy recovered.

Champalimaud said earlier this month that Totta and BPSM would retain separate identities in a group reorganisation that analysts interpreted as a drive to cut costs and boost the efficiency of the banking and insurance network.
Analysts said Champalimaud had a clearly defined strategy for his group including Totta, based on spreading risks across a range of financial services.
"You need to give it some time to see the Champalimaud group consolidate," said Midas's Guimaraes.
($1=153.5 escudos)
